newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Centralisation affects Gulf bank hub in Bahrain.
newsitem.headline: Centralisation affects Gulf bank hub in Bahrain.

text.p: Some Bahrain-based banks say business is still brisk in the Gulf's financial centre but others are cutting treasury operations in line with a trend to centralise in the age of sophisticated technology.
"We are doing very good business here," a senior official with an offshore banking unit (OBU) operating in Bahrain told Reuters. "Business is still very good".
But the number of OBUs which set up operations in the island state to cash in on the oil boom of the mid-1970s has been gradually dropping in recent years.
The Bahrain Monetary Agency, the central bank, says there were 46 OBUs operating from Bahrain in 1996 with total assets of $67 billion compared with 75 OBUs at the start of the oil boom.
OBU assets peaked at $72.58 billion at the end of 1989.
Bankers said some international banks had moved to cut their treasury operations in Bahrain, the Gulf's main financial and banking centre, to consolidate operations and cut costs.

The latest to make the move is Chase Manhattan Bank, part of the U.S. Chase Manhattan Corp. A bank official told Reuters on Monday that a single dealer would man Chase's Bahrain dealing room as of the end of July, down from six.
"The bank is moving dealing room control to London from Bahrain and cutting its staff," he added. Chase is a big player in major foreign and regional currencies from Bahrain.

Another banker said: "Banks are moving to consolidate operations. There is no question of commitment because modern technology makes it no difference if you are here or miles away...By consolidating, you operate more efficiently."
Some global giants have moved out although some bankers stress the need to stay close to clients to provide adequate services and generate new business in the oil-rich region.
Banque Indosuez moved its treasury department to London from Bahrain at the end of 1996.

Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) closed its Bahrain OBU in 1996 and investment bank Okasan International E.C., 51 percent owned by Okasan Securities of Japan, said this week it was liquidating its Bahrain office from July 1.
Saad Investment Company last month moved its entire investment operation to Geneva from Bahrain.

Bankers, however, still say Bahrain would maintain its position as the area's financial and banking hub in the face of competition from emerging regional centres because of its regulations and advanced services to the sector.

"Before we decided to launch a new bank we had a lengthy discussion. We found that Bahrain was the suitable place for banking activites," a senior official at a new bank which opened on the island earlier this year said.
"Bahrain has good banking experience and communications and above all the Bahrain Monetary Agency has a firm control over banking regulations," he added.
